<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Yann" />{{rh|196|AITAREYÂ-ARA''N''YAKA.|}}{{rule}}</noinclude>9. Then he recites the Ekapadâ ({{lang|sa-Latl|indro visva''m'' vi râ''g''ati}}), wishing, May I be everything at once, and may I thus finish the whole work of metres<ref>The Ekapadâ forms the last metre in this ceremony.</ref>.

10. In reciting the hymn {{lang|sa-Latl|indra''m'' vi''s''vâ avîv''ri''dhan}} (Rv. I, 11) he intertwines the first seven verses by intertwining their feet<ref>The first and last half-verses of the hymn are not to be intertwined. Of the remaining fourteen half-verses he joins, for instance, the fourth foot of the first verse with the second foot of the second verse, and so on. Comm.</ref>. There are seven prâ''n''as (openings) in the head, and he thus places seven prâ''n''as in the head. The eighth verse (half-verse) he does not intertwine<ref>Because nothing more follows. Comm.</ref>. The eighth is speech, and he thinks, May my speech never be intertwined with the other prâ''n''as. Speech therefore, though dwelling in the same abode as the other prâ''n''as, is not intertwined with them.

11. He recites the Virâ''g'' verses<ref>Rv. VII, 22, 1–6.</ref>. Verily, Virâ''g'' verses are food, and they thus serve for the gaining of food.

12. He ends with the hymn of Vasish''th''a<ref>Rv. VII, 24.</ref>, wishing, May I be Vasish''th''a!

13. But let him end with the fifth verse, {{lang|sa-Latl|esha stomo maha ugrâya vâhe}}, which, possessing the word mahat, is auspicious.

14. In the second foot of the fifth verse the word dhuri occurs. Verily, dhu''h'' (the place where the horse is fastened to the car) is the end (of the car). This day also is the end (of the sacrifice which lasts a whole year)<ref>The last day is the udayanîyâtirâtra. Comm.</ref>. Thus the verse is fit for the day.
